lesson.menu_desc: An exit interview with a customer who switched to a competitor, and a win-loss report that turns a lost account into one clear lesson -- third conditional (if + had + past participle, would have + past participle)
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 29 -- If We Had Known... One lost account and what would have changed
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Patrícia Xavier Lima Iwashita | Lesson 29 -- If We Had Known...
lesson.grammar_point: third conditional (if + had + past participle, would have + past participle)

listenings.text: Hi Patrícia, it is Karen. Thank you for doing the Harbor Health exit interview. I know it is not a nice call. Before you write the report, remember why we do this. A lost account is expensive, but a lost lesson is more expensive. So please write it with the third conditional, and be specific. Not: if we had worked harder, we would have kept them. That helps nobody. Write something like: if we had seen the budget cut in June, we would have offered a smaller plan. One condition, one result, one date. And please end with one thing that we will do differently from next month. Send it to me by Friday, and we will present it together at the team meeting.

Hi Patrícia, it is Tom. Karen told me about Harbor Health. I am sorry, I know how that feels. Last year I lost a logistics account in almost the same way. Their director changed in March, and nobody on my side noticed. If I had met the new director in the first month, I would have kept the account, I am sure. Since then, I have a simple rule: every time a sponsor changes, I book a meeting within two weeks. It takes one hour, and it has saved two renewals. Anyway, if you want a second pair of eyes on your report, send it to me before Friday. Happy to help.
